title: One Helm Value Puts Running Java Services on EKS onto the Splunk APM Map
description: One Helm value put two running Spring Boot services on the Splunk APM map with 0 pod restarts. With a second value, traces held both services across two nodes.
body:
You have Java services running on EKS, and you want them on a service map today. That usually means a team adds instrumentation and plans a rollout, and you wait.

One value on the Splunk OTel Collector chart let me skip that step. **Two running Spring Boot services appeared on the Splunk APM map, and all three pods in the lab stayed the same pods, with 0 restarts.** Splunk drew the line from `orders` to `inventory` too.

The docs say no restart is needed, so I checked it pod by pod in a throwaway AWS account, on Amazon Linux 2023, with the services on two different nodes.

> **TL;DR**
> - Running Java services reach the Splunk APM map with no change to the pod spec.
> - `obi.enabled=true` starts OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation (OBI) on every node.
> - I measured 2 of 2 services on the map and 0 restarts across 3 pods. With a second value on as well, 39 of 39 traces found in Splunk held both services, across two nodes. I have no trace number for the first value alone, and the section below explains why.
> - The whole run took 26.9 minutes.

## Why a first map usually waits for a rollout

A language agent gives you the deepest detail, and it's where I'd go next. It joins the JVM at startup, though, so the pods have to roll.

So I started from services with nothing attached, and OBI off:

```text
OBI pods running: 0
orders JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or OTEL settings: 0
orders Java agents loaded: 0
inventory JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or OTEL settings: 0
inventory Java agents loaded: 0
```

The Collector was already sending cluster metrics, and the map had neither service on it.

## Turning on OBI with chart 0.163.1

[OBI is a beta feature in Splunk Observability Cloud](https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-observability-cloud/manage-data/instrument-back-end-services/instrument-back-end-applications-to-send-spans-to-splunk-apm/instrument-an-application-using-obi). It runs as a DaemonSet and captures traces and request metrics with no code change or restart. The [chart turns it on with one value](https://github.com/signalfx/splunk-otel-collector-chart/blob/main/docs/zero-code-ebpf-instrumentation.md):

```bash
helm upgrade splunk-otel-collector splunk-otel-collector-chart/splunk-otel-collector \
  --version 0.163.1 --namespace splunk --reuse-values --set obi.enabled=true
```

Nothing in the `demo` namespace was edited. The chart brought OBI 0.15.2, and OBI's log listed both JVMs.

## Same pod UIDs before and after, and 2 services on the map

These pods had the same UIDs, start times and restart counts before OBI, after the first value and after the second:

```text
inventory  ca653889-b1a6-4447-936a-93d5e12206a2  0  2026-11-05T22:26:50Z
orders     f0c67713-a216-4a19-a520-9d124ff13fd2  0  2026-11-05T22:26:49Z
postgres   d2e39469-51ee-4d5a-ad27-b8f3ed5abfc2  0  2026-11-05T22:26:55Z
```

A replaced pod starts again at 0, so the UIDs matter as much as the counts. This is the map Splunk APM returned with only the first value on:

```text
-- service map from Splunk APM
  inventory inferred=false
  orders inferred=false
  load inferred=false
  load -> orders
  orders -> inventory
```

`load` is my test client. OBI covers every namespace by default, so it appeared as well.

## A second value, and 39 of 39 traces across two nodes

`orders` and `inventory` ran on different nodes, so a joined trace had to cross the network. OBI's [outgoing propagation is off by default](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/zero-code/obi/distributed-traces/), and this value turns it on:

```bash
helm upgrade splunk-otel-collector splunk-otel-collector-chart/splunk-otel-collector \
  --version 0.163.1 --namespace splunk --reuse-values \
  --set-string obi.env.OTEL_EBPF_BPF_CONTEXT_PROPAGATION=headers
```

The same pods carried on, again with 0 restarts. Of 48 sampled trace IDs, Splunk returned 39, and **all 39 held both services**. Here's one:

```text
sample trace from the propagation case: 07515449a2bc2d3973c9a54e05c5a3c3
  orders null GET /orders/{id} span=6d8b9deb02b22f67 parent=27bbfc90c12b0320
  orders null GET /stock/{id} span=abb1276d3baad92f parent=6d8b9deb02b22f67
  load null GET /orders/* span=27bbfc90c12b0320 parent=none
  inventory null GET /stock/{id} span=967bac47e7062f91 parent=abb1276d3baad92f
```

Follow the parents and you get `load`, `orders`, then `inventory`, one chain across two nodes.

With the first value alone, none of the 56 sampled IDs came back inside the same 90-second wait. That's unmeasured. It doesn't show those traces were separate, or that the second value was required, so I can give you the result with both values on, not a before and after.

## What to plan for before you roll it out

**Privileges.** My run printed `hostPID=true hostNetwork=true privileged=true`, which is the [chart's default](https://github.com/signalfx/splunk-otel-collector-chart/blob/main/docs/zero-code-ebpf-instrumentation.md). Check that against your cluster policy. The chart guide lists a reduced set of capabilities too.

**OBI's Java helper.** You add nothing to the pod spec, and OBI looks after its own helper for the JVMs it finds. OBI's log ties that helper to Java TLS telemetry. Both JVMs went from 0 Java agents loaded to 4 agent library mappings, but in this run the attach didn't finish on either one:

```text
level=WARN msg="unable to attach java agent to process, Java TLS telemetry will not work" ... pid=3886 error="java attach timed out"
level=WARN msg="unable to attach java agent to process, Java TLS telemetry will not work" ... pid=4090 error="java attach timed out"
```

So read the mapping as the library being there, not as a finished attach. These services speak plain HTTP, and everything above came through anyway. If yours use TLS, look for this line first. If you reduce OBI's capabilities, read [this OBI issue on non-root JVMs](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-ebpf-instrumentation/issues/3895).

**Latency.** I ran three load rounds on each side, at one request every 50 ms:

```text
p95 with OBI off: min 11.66, median 13.93, max 15.52 ms
p95 with OBI on: min 11.21, median 12.87, max 15.82 ms
```

The median moved by -1.06 ms and the ranges overlap, so I read that as no visible change at this load, not a speed-up. Every round finished with `errors=0`. CPU on the `orders` node read 9, 10 and 13 percent with OBI off, then 16, 10 and 11 with it on.

## Build it yourself in 3 steps

### Step 1: Create the cluster (about 8 minutes)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Abhimanyu9988/Abhimanyu9988.github.io.git
cd Abhimanyu9988.github.io/labs/one-helm-value-puts-running-java-service
export AWS_REGION=eu-central-1 LAB_NAME=obi-demo TF_VAR_lab_name=obi-demo
export SPLUNK_REALM=us1 SPLUNK_ACCESS_TOKEN=your-ingest-token SPLUNK_API_TOKEN=your-api-token
terraform init && terraform apply -auto-approve
```

### Step 2: Start the services with OBI off (about 4 minutes)

Run `./reproduce.sh`. It installs the Collector, starts the services and records each pod.

### Step 3: Turn on OBI and read the results (about 12 minutes)

Run `./fix.sh`. It sets the first value, reads the map, then runs `propagate.sh` for the second value and prints everything above.

## Use it for your own services

- **Use the first map to pick your next conversation.** It shows who calls whom before any team changes a deployment.
- **Test both values together for traces across nodes.** Try them on your own network path, because [proxies and load balancers can affect propagation](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/zero-code/obi/distributed-traces/), and check async frameworks [on their own](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/zero-code/obi/context-propagation/).
- **Keep language agents for depth.** [Splunk recommends combining them](https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-observability-cloud/manage-data/instrument-back-end-services/instrument-back-end-applications-to-send-spans-to-splunk-apm/instrument-an-application-using-obi), and OBI skips processes that already have OpenTelemetry instrumentation.

## Clean up (the cluster and nodes cost money while they run)

```bash
./cleanup.sh
terraform destroy -auto-approve
```

## What I didn't test

- **Other stacks.** This is two Spring Boot services on Java 21 over plain HTTP, on three `t3.large` nodes running Amazon Linux 2023. The [chart guide](https://github.com/signalfx/splunk-otel-collector-chart/blob/main/docs/zero-code-ebpf-instrumentation.md) names Ubuntu as its tested OS, so this adds one result on Amazon Linux 2023.
- **Database spans.** I didn't measure them, and Postgres wasn't on this map.
- **Traces with the first value alone**, as explained above.
- **TLS traffic, reduced capabilities or higher load.** Nothing here covers them.

Disclosure: I work at Splunk, part of Cisco. This is my personal writing; the post isn't sponsored or reviewed by my employer.

source_replies.text: For anyone comparing setups: I ran OBI 0.15.2 through the Splunk OTel Collector chart 0.163.1, which runs it privileged by default, against two Spring Boot services on EKS. Both JVMs showed the Java agent library mapped afterwards, and OBI logged java attach timed out for both. Those services use plain HTTP, and the map and traces came through. I didn't test TLS or reduced capabilities. I wrote up the full build here: https://showmerit.com/abhimanyu/articles/one-helm-value-puts-running-java-services-on-eks-onto-the/
